source_refs.note: 3.3 Trigonometric Substitution: Cases 1-3, special integrals (i)-(ii) with proofs, Challenge box, Examples 22-28 (book prints 23 twice, no 25; shown as 22-28)

blocks.text: Integrals involving the radicals \(\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\), \(\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}\), and \(\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}\) (where \(a > 0\)) can often be evaluated by making a substitution involving a trigonometric function. The objective of trigonometric substitution is to eliminate the radical in the integrand. We do this by using the Pythagorean identities:

blocks.text_alt: sine squared theta plus cosine squared theta equals 1, and secant squared theta minus tangent squared theta equals 1

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does a trigonometric function help? A square root is hard to integrate, but the square root of a perfect square is easy: \(\sqrt{p^{2}} = |p|\). The Pythagorean identities turn \(a^{2} - x^{2}\), \(a^{2} + x^{2}\) or \(x^{2} - a^{2}\) into a single square, so the root disappears.
For example, if \(x = a\sin\theta\) then \(a^{2} - x^{2} = a^{2}(1 - \sin^{2}\theta) = a^{2}\cos^{2}\theta\), and \(\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}} = a\cos\theta\).
The second identity can also be written \(1 + \tan^{2}\theta = \sec^{2}\theta\).
Case 1: Integrals involving \(\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\) (where, \(a > 0\)) can frequently be reduced to a simpler form by using the substitution \(x = a\sin\theta\).
Case 2: Integrals involving \(\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}\) (where, \(a > 0\)) can frequently be reduced to a simpler form by using the substitution \(x = a\tan\theta\).
Case 3: Finally, integrals involving \(\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}\) (where, \(a > 0\)) can frequently be reduced to a simpler form by using the substitution \(x = a\sec\theta\).

blocks.caption: Our summary of the three cases (not printed in the book)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to choose: look at the sign pattern under the root. Constant minus variable: \(\sin\). Constant plus variable: \(\tan\). Variable minus constant: \(\sec\).
The angle is kept in a fixed range so that the root is positive and the substitution can be reversed: Case 1 \(-\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}\) (\(\cos\theta \ge 0\)); Case 2 \(-\frac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}\) (\(\sec\theta > 0\)); Case 3 \(0 \le \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}\) when \(x \ge a\) (\(\tan\theta \ge 0\)).
At the end the answer must be written back in \(x\). A right triangle helps: from \(\sin\theta = \frac{x}{a}\) take opposite side \(x\), hypotenuse \(a\), adjacent side \(\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\), and read off any other ratio.
The same idea works when the expression is not exactly \(a^{2} \pm x^{2}\): complete the square or substitute first (see Examples 23 and 28).
Some Special Integrals as Formulae

blocks.text_alt: (i) integral of 1 over (a squared minus x squared) dx equals 1 over 2a times ln of modulus of (a plus x) over (a minus x), plus c
(ii) integral of 1 over square root of (a squared minus x squared) dx equals inverse sine of x over a, plus c, where a is greater than 0

blocks.text:
Proof: (i) We want to evaluate \(\int\frac{1}{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx\)
The denominator \(a^{2}-x^{2} = (a-x)(a+x)\), so
\[\int\dfrac{1}{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx = \int\dfrac{1}{(a-x)(a+x)}\,dx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2a}\int\dfrac{(a-x)+(a+x)}{(a-x)(a+x)}\,dx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2a}\int\Big[\dfrac{(a-x)}{(a-x)(a+x)}\]
\[\qquad + \dfrac{(a+x)}{(a-x)(a+x)}\Big]dx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2a}\int\left(\dfrac{1}{a+x} + \dfrac{1}{a-x}\right)dx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2a}\int\left(\dfrac{1}{a+x} - \dfrac{-1}{a-x}\right)dx\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2a}\big(\ln|a+x| - \ln|a-x|\big) + c\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\dfrac{a+x}{a-x}\right| + c\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The key trick: the numerator 1 is written as \(\frac{(a-x)+(a+x)}{2a}\), because \((a-x)+(a+x) = 2a\). This splits one hard fraction into two easy ones (this is partial fractions in disguise).
Why \(\int\frac{dx}{a-x} = -\ln|a-x|\)? The derivative of \(a - x\) is \(-1\), so \(\frac{-1}{a-x}\) is of the form \(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\) and integrates to \(\ln|a-x|\). That is why the book writes \(\frac{1}{a-x} = -\frac{-1}{a-x}\).
Finally \(\ln|A| - \ln|B| = \ln\left|\frac{A}{B}\right|\).

blocks.title: Challenge!
blocks.text:
Prove the given formulae.
(i) \(\int\frac{1}{x^{2}-a^{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right| + c\)
(ii) \(\int\frac{1}{a^{2}+x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + c\)
(iii) \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}} = \ln\left|x + \sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}\right| + c\), where \(a > 0\)
(iv) \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}} = \ln\left|x + \sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}\right| + c\), where \(a > 0\)
(v) \(\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}} = \frac{1}{a}\sec^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + c\), where \(a > 0\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Hints for the Challenge: (i) as in Proof (i), with \(1 = \frac{(x+a)-(x-a)}{2a}\). (ii) put \(x = a\tan\theta\). (iii) put \(x = a\tan\theta\) and use \(\int\sec\theta\,d\theta = \ln|\sec\theta + \tan\theta|\). (iv) put \(x = a\sec\theta\) and use the same \(\sec\theta\) integral. (v) put \(x = a\sec\theta\); the integral becomes \(\frac{1}{a}\int d\theta\).
In (iii) and (iv) a constant \(-\ln a\) appears; it is absorbed into \(c\).
Formula (v) as printed holds for \(x > a\). For \(x < -a\) write \(\frac{1}{a}\sec^{-1}\left|\frac{x}{a}\right| + c\) (the book does this in Example 28).
(ii) We want to evaluate \(\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}\,dx\), where \(a\) is a positive constant and the domain is \(-a < x < a\) so that the square root is real.

Let \(x = a\sin\theta\), \(-\frac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}\), then \(dx = a\cos\theta\,d\theta\). Also
\[\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}} = \sqrt{a^{2}-(a\sin\theta)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{a^{2}-a^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}\]
\[= \sqrt{a^{2}(1-\sin^{2}\theta)}\]
\[= \sqrt{a^{2}\cos^{2}\theta} = a|\cos\theta|\]
On the interval \(-\frac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\cos\theta > 0\), so \(|\cos\theta| = \cos\theta\). Thus, \(\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}} = a\cos\theta\).

Substitute into the integral:
\[\int\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}\,dx\]
\[= \int\dfrac{1}{a\cos\theta}\cdot a\cos\theta\,d\theta\]
\(= \int 1\,d = \theta + c\)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(\int 1\,d = \theta + c\): the variable of integration is missing. It should be \(\int 1\,d\theta = \theta + c\).

We have \(x = a\sin\theta \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \frac{x}{a}\), and since \(\theta\) is in the principal range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(\theta = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)\).
Thus, \(\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}\,dx = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + c\)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why must \(\theta\) stay in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\)? On this range \(\cos\theta \ge 0\), so \(\sqrt{a^{2}\cos^{2}\theta} = a\cos\theta\) without a minus sign, and \(\sin\theta = \frac{x}{a}\) has exactly one solution \(\theta = \sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a}\).
Notice how neat the result is: after the substitution the integrand became just 1. That is the power of choosing the right substitution.

blocks.title: Example 22
steps:
Given: \(\int\frac{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}{x^{2}}\,dx\)
To find: the indefinite integral.
Method: the radical is \(\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\) with \(a = 3\), so Case 1: put \(x = 3\sin\theta\). The identity \(1 - \sin^{2}\theta = \cos^{2}\theta\) removes the root.

Step 1: Substitute
\[x = 3\sin\theta,\quad dx = 3\cos\theta\,d\theta\]
with \(\theta \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)\cup\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).
Why: \(\theta \ne 0\) because \(x \ne 0\) (it is in the denominator); on this range \(\cos\theta \ge 0\).

Step 2: Remove the root
\[\sqrt{9-x^{2}} = \sqrt{9-(3\sin\theta)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{9(1-\sin^{2}\theta)} = \sqrt{9\cos^{2}\theta}\]
\[= 3\cos\theta\]
Why: \(1 - \sin^{2}\theta = \cos^{2}\theta\) and \(\cos\theta \ge 0\).

Step 3: Write the integral in \(\theta\)
\[\int\dfrac{3\cos\theta}{(3\sin\theta)^{2}}\cdot 3\cos\theta\,d\theta\]
\[= \int\dfrac{9\cos^{2}\theta}{9\sin^{2}\theta}\,d\theta = \int\cot^{2}\theta\,d\theta\]
Why: every \(x\) and \(dx\) has been replaced.

Step 4: Integrate
\[\int(\csc^{2}\theta - 1)\,d\theta = -\cot\theta - \theta + c \quad (1)\]
Why: \(\cot^{2}\theta = \csc^{2}\theta - 1\) and \(\int\csc^{2}\theta\,d\theta = -\cot\theta\).

Step 5: Back to \(x\)
\[\sin\theta = \dfrac{x}{3} \Rightarrow \theta = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\]
\[\cot\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\theta}}{\sin\theta} = \dfrac{\sqrt{1-\frac{x^{2}}{9}}}{\frac{x}{3}}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}{x}\]
Why: \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{1-\sin^{2}\theta}\) because \(\cos\theta \ge 0\); \(\sqrt{1 - \frac{x^{2}}{9}} = \frac{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}{3}\).

Step 6: Put into (1)
\[\int\dfrac{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}{x^{2}}\,dx\]
\[= -\dfrac{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}{x} - \sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3} + c\]
Why: the answer must be in \(x\).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big(-\dfrac{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}{x}\Big) = \dfrac{9}{x^{2}\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big(-\sin^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3}\Big) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}\]
Sum: \(\frac{9 - x^{2}}{x^{2}\sqrt{9-x^{2}}} = \frac{\sqrt{9-x^{2}}}{x^{2}}\), the integrand.

blocks.title: Example 23
steps:
Given: \(\int\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^{4}+1}}\,dx\)
To find: the indefinite integral.
Method: \(x^{4}+1 = (x^{2})^{2}+1\) has the form \(u^{2}+1\) with \(u = x^{2}\): Case 2, put \(x^{2} = \tan\theta\). To make \(d(x^{2}) = 2x\,dx\) appear, multiply and divide by \(2x\).

Step 1: Prepare the integrand
\[\int\dfrac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^{4}+1}}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{2x\,dx}{x^{2}\sqrt{(x^{2})^{2}+1}}\]
Why: \(\frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{2x}{x^{2}}\), so nothing has changed.

Step 2: Substitute
\[x^{2} = \tan\theta,\quad 2x\,dx = \sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta\]
The book takes \(\theta \in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\); since \(x^{2} > 0\), in fact \(0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}\).
Why: differentiate both sides; \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\tan\theta = \sec^{2}\theta\).

Step 3: Simplify
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{\sec^{2}\theta}{\tan\theta\sqrt{\tan^{2}\theta+1}}\,d\theta\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{\sec^{2}\theta}{\tan\theta\sec\theta}\,d\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\int\dfrac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta}\,d\theta\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\int\csc\theta\,d\theta\]
Why: \(\tan^{2}\theta + 1 = \sec^{2}\theta\) with \(\sec\theta > 0\), and \(\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta} = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}\cdot\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} = \csc\theta\).

Step 4: Integrate
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln|\csc\theta - \cot\theta| + c\]
Why: \(\int\csc\theta\,d\theta = \ln|\csc\theta - \cot\theta| + c\).

Step 5: Back to \(x\)
\[\cot\theta = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta} = \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\]
\[\csc\theta = \sqrt{1+\cot^{2}\theta} = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)^{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sqrt{x^{4}+1}}{x^{2}}\]
Why: \(1 + \cot^{2}\theta = \csc^{2}\theta\), and \(\csc\theta > 0\) for \(0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}\).

Step 6: Write the answer
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|\dfrac{\sqrt{x^{4}+1}}{x^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right| + c\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left|\dfrac{\sqrt{x^{4}+1}-1}{x^{2}}\right| + c\]
Why: same denominator \(x^{2}\).

Check:
Write the answer as \(\frac{1}{2}\ln(\sqrt{x^{4}+1}-1) - \ln|x|\). Its derivative is
\[\dfrac{x^{3}}{\sqrt{x^{4}+1}(\sqrt{x^{4}+1}-1)} - \dfrac{1}{x}\]
Multiplying the first fraction by \(\frac{\sqrt{x^{4}+1}+1}{\sqrt{x^{4}+1}+1}\) gives \(\frac{\sqrt{x^{4}+1}+1}{x\sqrt{x^{4}+1}}\); subtracting \(\frac{1}{x}\) leaves \(\frac{1}{x\sqrt{x^{4}+1}}\), the integrand.

blocks.title: Numbering note (ours)
blocks.text: The textbook prints the number 'Example 23' twice (first for \(\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{x^{4}+1}}\), then for \(\int\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}{x}\,dx\)) and has no Example 25. We show the second one as Example 24 and the book's Example 24 as Example 25, so that every example has its own number: 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28.

blocks.title: Example 24
steps:
Given: \(\int\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}{x}\,dx\), \(x > 3\)
To find: the indefinite integral.
Method: the radical is \(\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}\) with \(a = 3\): Case 3, put \(x = 3\sec\theta\). The identity \(\sec^{2}\theta - 1 = \tan^{2}\theta\) removes the root.

Step 1: Substitute
\[x = 3\sec\theta,\quad dx = 3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\]
Since \(x > 3\), \(0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\tan\theta > 0\).
Why: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\sec\theta = \sec\theta\tan\theta\).

Step 2: Write the integral in \(\theta\)
\[\int\dfrac{\sqrt{(3\sec\theta)^{2}-9}}{3\sec\theta}\cdot 3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\]
\[= \int\sqrt{9(\sec^{2}\theta-1)}\cdot\tan\theta\,d\theta\]
\[= \int 3\tan\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta = 3\int\tan^{2}\theta\,d\theta\]
Why: \(3\sec\theta\) cancels; \(\sqrt{9\tan^{2}\theta} = 3\tan\theta\).

Step 3: Integrate
\[= 3\int(\sec^{2}\theta - 1)\,d\theta = 3(\tan\theta - \theta) + c\]
Why: \(\tan^{2}\theta = \sec^{2}\theta - 1\).

Step 4: Back to \(x\)
\[\tan\theta = \sqrt{\sec^{2}\theta - 1} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)^{2} - 1}\]
\[\theta = \sec^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)\]
\[3\Big[\sqrt{\tfrac{x^{2}}{9}-1} - \sec^{-1}\tfrac{x}{3}\Big]\]
\[= \sqrt{x^{2}-9} - 3\sec^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3}\]
Why: \(3\sqrt{\frac{x^{2}-9}{9}} = \sqrt{x^{2}-9}\).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\sqrt{x^{2}-9} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}3\sec^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3} = \dfrac{9}{x\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}\]
Difference: \(\frac{x^{2}-9}{x\sqrt{x^{2}-9}} = \frac{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}{x}\), the integrand.

blocks.title: Example 25
steps:
Given: \(\int\frac{(x+1)e^{x}}{1+x^{2}e^{2x}}\,dx\)
To find: the indefinite integral.
Method: \(x^{2}e^{2x} = (xe^{x})^{2}\), and the numerator \((x+1)e^{x}\) is the derivative of \(xe^{x}\). So put \(u = xe^{x}\); the integral becomes \(\int\frac{du}{1+u^{2}}\).

Step 1: Choose \(u\)
\[u = xe^{x}\]
\[\dfrac{du}{dx} = xe^{x} + e^{x}(1) \Rightarrow du = (x+1)e^{x}\,dx\]
Why: product rule.

Step 2: Rewrite and integrate
\[\int\dfrac{(x+1)e^{x}}{1+(xe^{x})^{2}}\,dx = \int\dfrac{du}{1+u^{2}}\]
\[= \tan^{-1}u + c = \tan^{-1}(xe^{x}) + c\]
Why: \(\int\frac{du}{1+u^{2}} = \tan^{-1}u + c\) (Challenge formula (ii) with \(a = 1\)).

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}(xe^{x})\]
\[= \dfrac{(x+1)e^{x}}{1+x^{2}e^{2x}}\]
The integrand comes back.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Example 25 needs no trigonometric substitution: a plain substitution \(u = xe^{x}\) already gives the standard form \(\int\frac{du}{1+u^{2}} = \tan^{-1}u\). Always first look for an inner function whose derivative is present.

blocks.title: Example 26
steps:
Given: \(\int\frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-x^{3}}}\,dx\), \(x \in (-\infty, 0)\cup(0, 1)\)
To find: the indefinite integral.
Method: put \(u = \sqrt{1-x^{3}}\), which removes the root. Its differential needs \(-3x^{2}\,dx\), so first multiply and divide by \(-3x^{2}\).

Step 1: Prepare the integrand
\[\int\dfrac{dx}{x\sqrt{1-x^{3}}}\]
\[= -\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{-3x^{2}}{x^{3}\sqrt{1-x^{3}}}\,dx\]
Why: \(-\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{-3x^{2}}{x^{3}} = \frac{1}{x}\); the value is unchanged.

Step 2: Substitute
\[u = \sqrt{1-x^{3}} \Rightarrow u^{2} = 1 - x^{3}\]
\[2u\,du = -3x^{2}\,dx,\quad x^{3} = 1 - u^{2}\]
Why: squaring first makes the differentiation easy.

Step 3: Write in \(u\)
\[= -\dfrac{1}{3}\int\dfrac{2u}{(1-u^{2})u}\,du\]
\[= \dfrac{2}{3}\int\dfrac{du}{u^{2}-1^{2}}\]
Why: \(u\) cancels and \(-\frac{1}{1-u^{2}} = \frac{1}{u^{2}-1}\).

Step 4: Use the formula \(\int\frac{du}{u^{2}-a^{2}}\) with \(a = 1\)
\[= \dfrac{2}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2(1)}\ln\left|\dfrac{u-1}{u+1}\right| + c\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left|\dfrac{\sqrt{1-x^{3}}-1}{\sqrt{1-x^{3}}+1}\right| + c\]
Why: Challenge formula (i); then \(u = \sqrt{1-x^{3}}\) is put back.

Check:
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big[\tfrac{1}{3}\ln\left|\tfrac{u-1}{u+1}\right|\Big]\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{2}{u^{2}-1}\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx}\]
With \(u^{2} - 1 = -x^{3}\) and \(\frac{du}{dx} = \frac{-3x^{2}}{2u}\) this is \(\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{2}{-x^{3}}\cdot\frac{-3x^{2}}{2u} = \frac{1}{xu} = \frac{1}{x\sqrt{1-x^{3}}}\).

blocks.title: Example 27
steps:
Given: \(\int\frac{2x}{\sqrt{x^{4}+9}}\,dx\)
To find: the indefinite integral.
Method: \(x^{4} = (x^{2})^{2}\) and \(2x\,dx = d(x^{2})\), so put \(u = x^{2}\); the result is the Challenge formula (iii) with \(a = 3\).

Step 1: Substitute
\[u = x^{2},\quad du = 2x\,dx\]
\[\int\dfrac{2x\,dx}{\sqrt{x^{4}+9}} = \int\dfrac{du}{\sqrt{u^{2}+3^{2}}}\]
Why: the numerator is exactly \(du\).

Step 2: Use the formula
\[= \ln\left|u + \sqrt{u^{2}+3^{2}}\right| + c\]
\[= \ln\left|x^{2} + \sqrt{x^{4}+9}\right| + c\]
Why: \(\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{a^{2}+u^{2}}} = \ln|u + \sqrt{a^{2}+u^{2}}| + c\); then \(u = x^{2}\) is put back (the book's last line writes the \(u\)-integral on the left; it equals the given integral).

blocks.title: Example 28
steps:
Given: \(\int\frac{dx}{(x-2)\sqrt{x^{2}-4x+3}}\)
To find: the indefinite integral.
Method: complete the square under the root, then put \(u = x - 2\); the integral has the form \(\int\frac{du}{u\sqrt{u^{2}-a^{2}}}\) (Challenge formula (v)) with \(a = 1\).

Step 1: Complete the square
\[x^{2}-4x+3 = (x^{2}-4x+4) + 3 - 4\]
\[= (x-2)^{2} - 1\]
Why: half of the coefficient of \(x\) is \(-2\), and \((-2)^{2} = 4\) is added and subtracted.

Step 2: Substitute \(u = x - 2\), \(du = dx\)
\[\int\dfrac{dx}{(x-2)\sqrt{(x-2)^{2}-1}}\]
\[= \int\dfrac{du}{u\sqrt{u^{2}-1^{2}}}\]
Why: the factor outside the root is the same \(x - 2\).

Step 3: Use the formula with \(a = 1\)
\[= \dfrac{1}{1}\sec^{-1}\left|\dfrac{u}{1}\right| + c = \sec^{-1}|u| + c\]
Why: Challenge formula (v). The book writes \(|u|\): then the answer holds for \(u > 1\) and for \(u < -1\) (that is, \(x > 3\) or \(x < 1\)).

Step 4: Put \(x\) back
\[= \sec^{-1}|x-2| + c\]
Why: \(u = x - 2\).

Check:
For \(u > 1\): \(\frac{d}{du}\sec^{-1}u = \frac{1}{u\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\). For \(u < -1\): \(\frac{d}{du}\sec^{-1}(-u) = \frac{-1}{(-u)\sqrt{u^{2}-1}} = \frac{1}{u\sqrt{u^{2}-1}}\). Both give the integrand.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
\(\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\): \(x = a\sin\theta\); \(\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}\): \(x = a\tan\theta\); \(\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}\): \(x = a\sec\theta\).
Replace \(dx\) too: \(dx = a\cos\theta\,d\theta\), \(a\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta\) or \(a\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta\).
Special integrals to remember: \(\int\frac{dx}{a^{2}-x^{2}} = \frac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\frac{a+x}{a-x}\right| + c\), \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}} = \sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a} + c\), and the five Challenge formulae.
Before using a formula, bring the integrand to its exact form: substitute (\(u = e^{x}\), \(u = \ln x\), \(u = x^{2}\)) or complete the square.
Always write the final answer back in \(x\), using a right triangle for the other ratios.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Forgetting to change \(dx\): \(x = 3\sin\theta\) needs \(dx = 3\cos\theta\,d\theta\), not \(d\theta\).
Mixing up the two log formulas: \(a^{2} - x^{2}\) gives \(\frac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\frac{a+x}{a-x}\right|\), while \(x^{2} - a^{2}\) gives \(\frac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right|\).
Writing \(\sqrt{a^{2}\cos^{2}\theta} = a\cos\theta\) without checking that \(\cos\theta \ge 0\) on the chosen range.
Leaving the answer in \(\theta\), or writing \(\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a^{2}}\) instead of \(\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a}\).
